title: Business judgment: Local evidence tempers generic AI advice
desc: Advocates human-led testing grounded in representative operational evidence, distinguishing plausible recommendations from demonstrated commercial productivity.

kps.k: The cluster concerns AI-assisted business judgement, not demonstrated productivity gains.
kps.d: The supplied Kenya field-experiment excerpts show advice exchanges and an entrepreneur’s qualitative report; the education-gap experiment excerpts supply business-diagnosis tasks and follow-up questions. Together, they illustrate how AI might support strategy and analysis while people supply context and decide what to implement. Neither set of excerpts reports treatment effects, establishes that AI improves business performance, or shows whether it narrows education-based productivity gaps.

kps.k: Local knowledge challenges generic growth advice and prompts more cautious recommendations.
kps.d: In the Kenya exchanges, the assistant proposes differentiation, loyalty rewards, referrals and community engagement. The entrepreneur questions whether distinctive meals would price out customers, whether community activities require excessive resources, and whether menu changes would alienate regulars. The assistant responds with affordable ingredients, smaller portions, low-cost rewards and gradual menu trials. This is a disagreement within an advice exchange about commercial fit, not a disagreement between studies about AI effectiveness; the predicted benefits remain unquantified.

kps.k: Sound diagnosis requires representative evidence and attention to operational detail.
kps.d: The Kenya entrepreneur warns that passengers in transit may give feedback that does not represent regular demand; the assistant recommends consulting regular customers and observing orders and leftovers. The education-gap task materials similarly require care with denominators and averages. Cafeteria-use rates apply only to employees present, so equal headcounts need not imply equal lunch demand when staffing composition and attendance rules differ. In the delivery exercise, preparation takes 29 minutes at North versus 18 at South, while North’s grill staff have much shorter tenure despite higher overall staff tenure. These facts motivate attendance and preparation hypotheses, not proven diagnoses: the supplied excerpts omit the sales and order-volume graphs needed for fuller analysis.

kps.k: The practical approach is human-led testing and review, with commercial outcomes kept distinct from plausible advice.
kps.d: The Kenya assistant recommends comparing trial dishes with existing items, reviewing feedback, monitoring retention and sales, and checking costs against revenues. It pairs expansion options such as delivery and catering with margin, inventory and waste controls; these remain proposals rather than demonstrated outcomes. The entrepreneur retains implementation authority through team deliberation. In the education-gap materials, the assistant knows only the attached report, and follow-up questions revisit participants’ explanations one week later. Those design features make information limits and retained understanding relevant, but the excerpts provide no results showing how well participants managed either.

vlens.an: The selected academia-and-research sources support the proposition that AI-assisted business judgment should remain human-led, locally grounded and empirically tested, while plausible advice must not be mistaken for demonstrated productivity. Their common reasoning is that generic recommendations and initial diagnoses are constrained by the evidence available: relevant customer feedback may be unrepresentative, and operational explanations require attention to denominators, workflow stages, staffing composition and role-specific experience. Material variation lies in the type of evidence. The Kenya field-experiment excerpts show an entrepreneur using local knowledge to qualify AI advice and retaining authority over implementation through pilots, monitoring and team deliberation. The randomized-experiment excerpts instead provide bounded diagnostic exercises and an assistant restricted to an attached report; they contain no reported treatment effects, so their support is methodological rather than evidence that AI improved performance or narrowed education-based gaps. This assessment applies only to the curated sources supplied, not to academia and research generally.

elens.an: The selected 2026 sources support the proposition that AI-assisted business judgment should remain human-led and grounded in representative local and operational evidence, while plausible advice must be distinguished from demonstrated productivity. Their common reasoning is that AI operates with incomplete context: generic recommendations can overlook affordability, customer composition and implementation risk, while business diagnoses can be distorted by inappropriate denominators, aggregate averages or missing workflow data. Material variation lies in how they make this case. The Kenya field-experiment excerpts show an entrepreneur actively correcting generic advice and retaining implementation authority, after which the assistant recommends pilots, monitoring and adjustment. The randomized-experiment excerpts instead provide bounded diagnostic tasks and an assistant limited to an attached report; because the supplied material contains no treatment-effect results, it supports epistemic caution rather than establishing AI’s commercial or education-gap effects. This assessment concerns only the curated sources supplied for the period and does not indicate the prevalence of this view among 2026 sources generally.
